blocks.text: Ask anyone who went to school in Turkey about the country's geography and you will hear about seven regions, *yedi bölge*. They were drawn at the First Geography Congress, held in Ankara in June 1941, where geographers divided the country by its landforms, climate, plants, farming and settlement. Four regions are named after the seas they border; the other three after their place in Anatolia. The congress also split them into smaller sections, 21 in all.

One feature of the map explains much of the difference between them. High mountain ranges run along the coasts, parallel to the sea, in the north and in the south. They catch the moist air coming off the water, so the coasts are green and wet, while the plateau behind them stays dry, with hot summers and cold winters.

**Karadeniz**, the Black Sea region, is a long strip of steep green mountains along the north coast. It gets more rain than any other region and has the most forest; on its eastern hills, around Rize, grows the tea of [A1 unit 6](a1-u06-culture).
**Marmara**, around the small Sea of Marmara, joins Europe and Asia. It is one of the smallest regions but by far the most populated, with Istanbul at its heart.

**Ege**, the Aegean region, has the longest coastline, and İzmir is its main city. **Akdeniz**, the Mediterranean region, has the warmest year and the mildest winters; its coast around Antalya is covered in greenhouses, more than anywhere else in the country.

Inland, **İç Anadolu**, Central Anatolia, is a high plateau of steppe and wheat fields around Ankara, and the driest region of all. **Doğu Anadolu**, Eastern Anatolia, is the largest region, about a fifth of the country, and also the highest and the coldest, with long, hard winters. Turkey's highest mountain, Ağrı Dağı (Mount Ararat, 5,137 m), and its largest lake, Van Gölü (Lake Van), are both there. **Güneydoğu Anadolu**, Southeastern Anatolia, is the smallest region, with the hottest and driest summers and the most hours of sunshine.

The regions are not administrative units: Turkey is governed through its 81 provinces. But they are the frame of every geography lesson, and a quick way to say where someone comes from: people talk of a *Karadenizli* or an *Egeli*, a man or woman from the Black Sea or the Aegean, and the regions are a natural map for the [regional cuisines](a2-u10-culture) of a later unit.

blocks.tr: Türkiye'de yedi bölge var. En büyük bölge Doğu Anadolu, en küçük bölge Güneydoğu Anadolu. Karadeniz'de en çok yağmur yağar. İç Anadolu Karadeniz'den çok daha kuru. Kışın en soğuk bölge Doğu Anadolu, en sıcak bölge Akdeniz. En kalabalık bölge Marmara, çünkü Türkiye'nin en büyük şehri İstanbul orada.
blocks.en: There are seven regions in Turkey. The largest region is Eastern Anatolia, the smallest Southeastern Anatolia. The Black Sea region gets the most rain. Central Anatolia is much drier than the Black Sea region. In winter, the coldest region is Eastern Anatolia and the warmest is the Mediterranean. The most crowded region is Marmara, because Turkey's biggest city, Istanbul, is there.

questions.q: When were the seven regions drawn?
questions.explain: At the First Geography Congress in Ankara, in June 1941.

questions.q: In the Turkish text, why is Marmara the most crowded region?
questions.explain: *çünkü Türkiye'nin en büyük şehri İstanbul orada*: **because Turkey's biggest city, Istanbul, is there**.

sources.title: Türkiye'nin coğrafi bölgeleri nasıl belirlenmişti?
sources.note: The First Turkish Geography Congress, 6–21 June 1941; physical, human and economic criteria; seven regions and 21 sub-regions, four named after seas and three after their position; Doğu Anadolu the largest (about 21%), Güneydoğu Anadolu the smallest (about 7.5%), Marmara the most populous

sources.title: First Geography Congress, Turkey
sources.note: Held in Ankara in 1941; seven regions still in use; four coastal regions named after their seas, three named after their position in Anatolia; the mountain ranges parallel to the coasts that shield the interior from the sea

sources.title: Geographical regions of Turkey
sources.note: Black Sea: highest precipitation, largest forest area; Aegean: longest coastline; Mediterranean: highest annual temperature, mildest winters, most greenhouse farming; Central Anatolia: lowest precipitation; Eastern Anatolia: largest area, highest elevation, coldest winters; Southeastern Anatolia: hottest and driest summers, most sunshine; Marmara: largest population

sources.title: Mount Ararat
sources.note: Ağrı Dağı, in extreme eastern Turkey; Great Ararat is the highest peak in Turkey

sources.title: Mount Ararat
sources.note: Greater Ararat 5,137 m, the highest peak in Turkey, in Iğdır and Ağrı provinces

sources.title: Lake Van
sources.note: The largest body of water in Turkey, in the eastern Anatolian highlands
